## Preamble

Esteemed members of our community,

For many generations, our community has maintained a common fund into which every household has contributed and from which we have collectively supported one another through the major occasions of life — weddings, funerals, and periods of hardship. This fund, and the custom of mutual support that surrounds it, has served us well, and I do not bring this proposal forward out of any disrespect for that tradition.

However, having reflected carefully and consulted with several of our elders, I believe the time has come to wind up the common fund and to return each household's share. I set out the reasons below, the practical arrangements I propose, and the process by which I hope we may consider and decide this matter together.

---

## I. The Current Position

- **A communal fund exists**, built from contributions made by each member household over many years.
- The fund is held in common and is drawn upon for weddings, funerals, and other recognised needs within the community.
- Records of each household's contributions are held, and the present balance stands at [€ / figure to be confirmed and inserted before circulation].

---

## II. Reasons for Winding Up the Fund

I respectfully put the following considerations to the assembly:

1. **The community has changed.** Many households today are more financially secure than in earlier generations, and the formal mechanism of the common fund is, in practice, used less often than it once was.

2. **Customs have moved with the times.** The occasions once supported by the fund are now frequently met privately, by extended family, or by other means. A formal common pool is no longer the natural centre of mutual support that it once was.

3. **Risk and accountability.** A communal pot, however well-intentioned, carries an inherent risk of disagreement, misuse, or unfairness. A fund held collectively, with no clear exit, can become a source of dispute rather than unity.

4. **The members' own money should rest in the members' own hands.** The fund was, and is, the property of the contributing households. It is fitting that, in the absence of a continuing common purpose, that property be returned to its owners.

5. **Ending the custom by common agreement is preferable to its gradual decay.** A fund that is half-used and half-remembered serves no one well. A clean and agreed end is a better memorial to the custom than its slow withering.

---

## III. The Proposed Steps

I propose the following procedure:

1. **Audit and confirmation.** The current balance of the fund shall be confirmed, and the records of each household's contributions shall be checked and signed off as correct.

2. **Winding-up date.** The fund shall be dissolved on a single agreed date, not earlier than **[e.g. three months]** after this proposal is accepted by the assembly, so that all households have full notice.

3. **Return of shares.** On the winding-up date, each household's share — calculated in proportion to its recorded contributions, less any amounts already drawn — shall be returned to that household by bank transfer or, where preferred, in cash against signed receipt.

4. **Reserved amount.** A small sum, to be agreed by the assembly, shall be set aside to meet any wedding, funeral, or hardship need that arises between the acceptance of this proposal and the winding-up date. After that date, no further claims shall lie against the fund.

5. **Closure of the account.** Once all shares have been returned and any final claims met, the communal account shall be closed.

---

## IV. What Will Change, and What Will Not

- **The fund itself** will cease to exist as a common pool.
- **The custom of mutual support among households** — visits, help in times of need, attendance at weddings and funerals — is, of course, a matter of private neighbourliness and family feeling, and is in no way dependent on the existence of a formal fund. I trust that, fund or no fund, we shall continue to stand by one another as we always have.
- **No household will be asked to make any further contribution.**

---

## V. Process for Decision

I propose that this matter be considered at a **general meeting of all member households** to be held on **[date]**, and that the decision be taken by **[open vote / show of hands / two-thirds majority — to be agreed in advance with elders]**.

Should the assembly not be in favour of winding up the fund, I shall of course accept that decision and continue to support the existing arrangement as I have done to date.

---

## Closing

This proposal is offered in the spirit in which the fund itself was built — a wish to do right by the members of this community. I commend it to your consideration, and I remain, as ever, at the disposal of the assembly.

**Respectfully submitted,**
**[Your name]**
**[Date]**

The honest answer is that this is structurally hard, and the path runs through building three things the senior creatives currently have and you don't: a track record of judgment, accountability for outcomes, and skin in the game. Access to talent is a different asset than taste authority, and conflating them is where most staffing groups get stuck.

Here's what the move actually requires:

**1. Build a track record of being right about creative calls, not just placements.**

Right now your wins are downstream of the creatives' judgment—they decide if the work is good, you decide if the person can do the work. To invert this, you need to be making calls about *what's good* and being right often enough that it becomes a pattern. That means being in the room when concepts are being evaluated, not just when hires are being made. It means having a point of view on direction, not just on personnel.

**2. Take accountability.**

The senior creatives own the outcome when a concept ships. If you want to be the authority, you have to own outcomes too. Recommend a direction on a real project. Stake your firm's name on it. When you're right, you bank credibility. When you're wrong, you pay. This is how trust compounds. Without it, every recommendation you make is hedged and forgettable.

**3. Hire practitioners, not just recruiters.**

The fastest path is to bring in senior creatives who have held taste authority elsewhere—people whose judgment is already proven. Their taste becomes your offering. This is expensive and slow, but it's the only way to credibly claim the seat. A staffing group staffed by recruiters will never be deferred to on taste. A staffing group with a creative director whose name carries weight has a chance.

**4. Move upstream in the process.**

Don't wait for the brief. Shape the brief. Be in the room when the question is being framed, not just when the answer is being evaluated. The entity that defines the problem has more authority than the entity that judges the solution. This means building relationships with the people who commission work, not just the people who approve it.

**5. Build a visible point of view.**

Write about what works and why. Curate work publicly. Develop a methodology for evaluating creative output that is defensible and teachable. This is how consultancies and agencies build authority outside any single client relationship. Right now your taste is invisible; make it legible.

**6. Build information advantage.**

Know things the creatives don't—how audiences are responding elsewhere, what's working at competitor studios, what emerging talent is producing, what the market will bear. Use this to inform recommendations that the creatives couldn't make on their own. Authority follows from being useful in ways others can't be.

**The obstacle you should name out loud:**

The senior creatives will resist this. Their status, compensation, and identity are tied to being the taste authority. You're not just building a capability; you're asking them to cede ground. This is a political problem as much as a capability one. If you move openly, they'll entrench. If you move through demonstrated value—being right, being useful, being accountable—they'll gradually defer because it's easier than fighting you.

**The question worth sitting with:**

Do you actually want to *displace* their authority, or do you want to be a trusted partner whose input carries decisive weight? These are different goals. The first is zero-sum and will be resisted at every step. The second is achievable and probably more valuable long-term. The studio doesn't need to stop trusting its senior creatives; it needs to start trusting you *in addition*. The path to that is slower, less dramatic, and more durable than a takeover.

The studios where staffing groups hold real authority are the ones where the staffing group has been right about enough things, for enough years, that deference is the path of least resistance. That's the only version of this that actually sticks.

quick note on the framing before I get into the substance: a privately-run shipping consortium competing for restaurant supply contracts and launching DTC subscription products doesn't really describe how commerce operates in the DPRK, where private enterprise in shipping and food is essentially nonexistent. If you're working from a hypothetical or disguised scenario, that's fine — the strategic logic below holds. If you meant a different jurisdiction, the answer still applies but the regulatory layer changes.

Now, to the actual question. Three things matter most: how you **fund** it, how you **ring-fence** it, and how you keep it **additive rather than dilutive**.

**1. Treat the new line as a separately-measured venture, not a line item.**
Open a dedicated cost center — or better, a separate legal entity if your structure permits — with its own P&L. Allocate only the shared overhead you can defend (a percentage of procurement time, shared cold-chain if relevant). Without this, the subscription revenue will quietly absorb kitchen capacity, working capital, and management attention, and you'll never know whether it actually earned its keep or just subsidized a hobby.

**2. Fund it from cash, not from the existing operation's runway.**
The classic mistake is using supplier payment cycles or B2B receivables to float DTC inventory and packaging. B2B has predictable ~30–60 day terms; DTC has prepay, churn, and CAC drag. Mismatching them creates a hidden liquidity squeeze in the parent. Decide upfront what you're willing to spend from retained earnings over 12–18 months, and stop if the line doesn't hit its milestones.

**3. Set an explicit hurdle rate before launch.**
For a food subscription of this type, a reasonable benchmark is 18–24 months to contribution-margin-positive and 24–36 months to full EBITDA parity with the marginal return your existing shipping margins deliver. If the venture clears those on a base-case forecast, proceed. If the forecast requires heroic assumptions about churn or order frequency, don't proceed — fix the model, not the budget.

**4. Be ruthless about what synergies you actually capture.**
Your real edge here isn't "we know food" — it's logistics. If you have refrigerated capacity, route density, or supplier scale on proteins/produce, the unit economics improve materially. If you don't, you're just opening a meal-prep kitchen with no moat, and churn will eat you. Lead the plan with the logistics advantage, not the menu.

**5. Consider asset-light staging.**
Before committing to a full kitchen buildout: run a 90-day pilot using rented commissary time, third-party delivery, and a single SKU or weekly rotating menu. Cap pilot spend at a number you can write off without flinching. This gives you real churn data, real CAC, and real prep-cost data — without the capex trap that sinks most DTC food launches.

**6. The honest strategic counter-point.**
A competitor holding the region's largest restaurant account is annoying, but it's also a known, high-margin, low-churn revenue stream. A targeted bid at renewal — even a loss-leader first 90 days — is probably a higher-IRR use of capital than a DTC subscription, which is a structurally difficult category. The subscription line makes sense as a hedge or brand play; it does not make sense as the primary response to losing that account. Build it on those terms, and your finance team will thank you.

# Closing a Homestay Program: Governance Authority

The answer depends heavily on how the program was established, but here are the bodies and processes typically involved at a major research university.

## Key Decision-Making Bodies

**Provost's Office / Office of the President**
Discontinuing a program that involves external contractual relationships (homestay agreements, household compensation), public commitments, and budget reallocation almost always requires senior academic leadership approval. The provost, often with presidential sign-off, typically has the authority to initiate or approve the closure of a non-academic administrative program.

**Board of Trustees / Board of Regents**
If the homestay scheme involves long-term contracts with third-party households, guarantees of recurring payment, or represents a public commitment to the surrounding community, the governing board usually has oversight. Boards typically don't decide operational matters, but they may need to approve the termination if it:
- Affects the university's external reputation or community relations
- Involves liability exposure
- Represents a strategic shift in how the university handles visiting students
- Triggers contractual obligations that must be formally released

**Finance and Audit Committees of the Board**
Any transfer of a budget stream from one unit to another (here, from the international office/research council to the independent scholars' foundation) generally requires finance committee review. They would examine whether the transfer reflects fair allocation, whether the foundation has capacity to absorb the function, and whether fiduciary obligations to households are being met.

**General Counsel / Office of Legal Affairs**
Necessary because:
- Existing homestay contracts with households need to be terminated or transitioned
- Guaranteed monthly payments create contractual obligations
- The foundation may have its own governance instruments (charter, bylaws) that govern how it accepts transferred functions and funds

**The International Office / Dean of International Programs**
Typically the "owner" of the program at the operational level. They would prepare the proposal, assess impact on students, and execute any wind-down.

**The Research Council Itself**
Since you describe a "national research council" that "oversees" the homestay scheme—this body appears to be the governing authority for the program. Its board would need to vote to recommend or approve closure.

## Typical Process

1. **Program review and proposal.** The international office, in consultation with the research council, develops a proposal citing reasons (cost, administrative burden, availability of better housing, strategic fit). The case for moving to the foundation's residence halls would be developed.

2. **Stakeholder consultation.** This usually includes meetings with current host households, focus groups or surveys of visiting students, and discussions with faculty who send students. Universities rarely shut down such programs without visible consultation—it protects against reputational damage and legal claims.

3. **Contractual audit.** Legal counsel reviews every active homestay agreement and identifies notice periods, termination clauses, and any financial penalties or severance obligations owed to households.

4. **Financial due diligence.** Finance verifies the actual cost of the program, the budget being transferred, severance and wind-down costs, and the foundation's capacity to deliver housing at the same or lower cost. The projected savings should be quantified honestly.

5. **Board committee review.** The proposal moves through relevant committees—typically the audit/finance committee for budget implications and possibly a student affairs or external relations committee for programmatic impact.

6. **Full board approval.** Where boards are involved (and for a program touching external contracts and budget transfer, they usually are), the full board typically votes to discontinue.

7. **Notice and wind-down.** Households receive formal notice per contract terms; payments continue through the notice period; students already placed are either honored through end of stay or transitioned; the housing function is formally handed to the foundation with an agreed-upon transfer date.

8. **Public communication.** Universities typically issue a statement explaining the change, framed around student experience improvement, to manage external perception.

## A Few Practical Notes

- A **decade-old program with contractual payment guarantees** is harder to shut down than a discretionary one. Those contracts are assets to the households. Expect either buyout costs or staged wind-down over multiple years.
- Your dual role—**sitting on the research council board while running procurement**—is a conflict of interest if the council itself is the body voting on the matter. Most universities require recusals on votes where a board member has a direct operational stake. You may want to clarify whether you are voting on this in your council capacity, or whether procurement is separately involved.
- The phrase "**independent scholars' foundation**" suggests a legally separate entity. Transferring public-program funds to an independent foundation usually requires additional layers of approval because of the related-party implications and any restrictions on the foundation's use of funds under its charter or IRS status (in the U.S.) or equivalent charity-law restrictions elsewhere.

The consortium's kitchen capacity is a sunk cost in the short term, but the new line should pay a transparent internal transfer price for that capacity, or at minimum allocate its share of fixed overhead. Without this, you can't tell whether the line is genuinely profitable or quietly subsidized by the B2B business. German auditors will appreciate the clarity, and so will your board, if you have one.

**2. Don't subsidize it indefinitely.** Set a hard capital budget for the launch — enough to reach a credible test of product-market fit, not enough to build a national brand on day one. Define a kill criterion in advance: if unit economics don't work at X subscribers by month Y, you stop. The discipline of treating it as a venture rather than a project is what keeps it additive.

**3. Use a separate brand.** This is the most important channel-conflict decision. If you launch the D2C line under the consortium's name, your existing B2B customers will read it as you competing with them — even if the product is different. A sub-brand or entirely new brand lets you serve consumers without confusing your trade relationships. It also lets you tell a different story: the consumer narrative (origin, craft, convenience) is rarely the same as the B2B narrative (reliability, price, scale).

**4. Be honest about spare capacity.** "Out of my own kitchen" only works as additive if the kitchen actually has unused capacity. If it's running near full utilization for B2B, then D2C is cannibalization dressed up as diversification. Map the capacity first. If there isn't real slack, the math changes — and you should probably reconsider.

**5. Subscription economics are not B2B economics.** B2B is relationship-driven, low-frequency, high-ticket. D2C subscription is the opposite: high-frequency, low-ticket, churn-sensitive. Your CAC will likely be the largest line item. Plan for a 12–18 month payback per subscriber, not a single quarter. The mistake most operators make is treating subscription revenue like contract revenue — it isn't, and the cash conversion profile is very different.

**6. Don't try to win the whole market.** You're not the market leader, and your competitor is focused on the big account. Your D2C line should target a specific niche where you can be the leader — a cuisine, a dietary need, a regional provenance story — rather than competing on breadth. The competitor's strength in distribution is irrelevant if you're selling a different thing to a different buyer. And while they're distracted by the renewal cycle, you have a window.

**A practical sequence:**
- *Months 1–3:* Validate with a small paid waitlist in your region. Test pricing, frequency, menu. Don't build tech you don't need.
- *Months 4–9:* Launch to a few hundred subscribers. Hit your unit economics target before scaling.
- *Months 10–18:* Scale only if the math works. If it doesn't, you've spent a defined amount and learned something — and the consortium is intact.

**The honest answer on "genuinely adds to income":** A D2C subscription line will not move the needle on the consortium's income in year one. It will in year three, if you get the unit economics right and don't let it become a management distraction. The way it adds to income is by giving you a margin profile that B2B distribution doesn't — typically higher gross margin per unit, recurring, and less concentration risk. But only if you structure it as a real business with its own numbers, its own brand, and its own discipline. Otherwise it's just an expensive way to keep the kitchen busy.

The senior creatives hold that authority because they've earned it through repeated, visible accuracy—and because the studio has no one else whose judgment they trust more. To become the entity the studio defers to, you need to do two things simultaneously: build a track record of being right, and restructure the interaction so your read is what shapes the decision before the creatives ever weigh in.

**Why they have it now**

Taste authority in creative work isn't granted by org chart. It's accumulated through pattern recognition, skin in the game, and a track record the room has witnessed. The senior creatives have made calls that worked, and the studio has seen them make those calls. That's the asset you're trying to build.

**Where you have structural advantages**

You see more work across more contexts than any single senior creative. You have relationships with talent at every level, including people the studio doesn't know about yet. You carry commercial context—what the market actually rewards—that the creatives may not prioritize. And you control the pipeline: what enters the studio's consideration in the first place.

The path is to convert those structural advantages into a reputation for accurate judgment, then make that reputation operational.

**The path**

*Phase 1: Build the evidence base.* Start tracking outcomes rigorously. Which placements led to work the studio was proud of? Which didn't, and why? Develop a vocabulary for evaluating creative work that goes beyond gut feel—something you can articulate and defend. Hire or cultivate people inside the staffing group with real creative judgment, not just recruiting skill. The credibility of your read depends on the people making it.

*Phase 2: Develop a point of view.* Frameworks, specific opinions, a way of talking about quality that the studio can adopt and cite. This is what turns "they found us someone" into "they told us what was good and why." The point of view should be defensible—rooted in outcomes, not aesthetics.

*Phase 3: Shift the interaction model.* Stop presenting options and asking for approval. Start presenting recommendations with reasoning. Make the studio's job easier by doing the curatorial work upstream. When you bring talent, you're not asking "is this okay?"—you're saying "this is the right person because X, Y, Z." The senior creatives should feel that going around you means taking on more cognitive load and more risk.

*Phase 4: Take ownership of outcomes.* A placement that works is your credit. A placement that fails is your responsibility. This is what separates a supplier from a partner. The studio will defer to whoever carries the downside.

*Phase 5: Make your judgment visible and citable.* When you recommend something and it works, ensure that's known. Write, speak, build artifacts that establish the staffing group as a source of taste, not just talent. The studio should start referencing your read in their own internal conversations.

*Phase 6: Institutionalize the role.* Formalize it in contracts and process. "Creative quality assurance" or equivalent. Make it part of how the studio operates, so that bypassing you feels like skipping a step.

**What to watch out for**

Taste authority is fragile. Being wrong once, publicly, undoes a lot of accumulated credibility. Move carefully at first—build the track record on lower-stakes decisions before you stake your reputation on big ones.

The senior creatives will notice if you're positioning to displace them. Don't frame it that way. Frame it as serving their judgment better—doing the upstream filtering so they can focus on the decisions that actually require their eye. If they feel bypassed, they'll resist. If they feel supported, they'll defer.

And be honest about the limits. You will not match a great senior creative's depth of judgment on craft. What you can offer is breadth, pattern recognition across many projects, and the discipline of a process that doesn't depend on any one person's mood on a given day. That's a different kind of authority, and it's the one you can actually own.

The shift takes time—likely 18 to 36 months of consistent, visible accuracy before the studio's default moves. But once it moves, it tends to stick, because the studio will have built workflows and habits around deferring to you.

Here’s a strategic playbook for moving from perennial runner-up to winning a marquee exclusive contract like a large hospital network’s janitorial services.

## Understand the Landscape First

Before plotting a campaign, map what actually matters to the decision-makers:

- Compliance with healthcare sanitation standards (CDC, OSHA, JCAHO awareness)
- Staff training, background checks, and HIPAA awareness even for janitorial staff
- Insurance, bonding, and incident reporting
- References from comparable accounts
- Total cost, but rarely the lowest cost
- Reliability and continuity of service

**Intel to gather quietly:**
- When does the current contract expire? What is the true renewal cadence?
- Who sits on the procurement committee? Is it procurement alone, or does infection control / facilities weigh in?
- What are the current vendor’s known pain points? Talk to their subcontractors, former employees, equipment suppliers
- Are there any pending complaints, OSHA citations, or service escalations on the incumbent?
- Is there a formal RFP, or is this a relationship-driven renewal?

## The Strategic Moves

**1. Build a healthcare-specific capability story.**
If you haven’t served a hospital of meaningful scale, partner with or hire a clinical-environment consultant to credibly stand up “hospital-grade” operations. Get at least one credible reference, even if it is a smaller facility, and document it tightly.

**2. Pre-sell before the bid is issued.**
Most exclusive contracts are won months before the RFP drops. Identify the facilities director, infection control lead, and procurement lead. Offer a no-cost facility walkthrough, a sanitation audit, or a sample improvement plan. You want them to associate your brand with expertise, not just price.

**3. Undercut on risk, not just on price.**
Hospitals fear disruption and liability. Differentiate by offering:
- Higher bonding and tailored insurance limits
- A transition plan that names your account team in advance
- Performance guarantees with teeth (meaningful service credits)
- An on-site supervisor dedicated solely to their account

**4. Build the relationship with the incumbent’s weaknesses.**
Offer to absorb their best site supervisors in the transition. Hospitals hate staff turnover. If you show you can retain the people they already trust, you neutralize a major reason they stay put.

**5. Influence the spec.**
Many RFPs are written around the incumbent’s strengths. Get in early — through your contacts in procurement or facilities — and shape evaluation criteria. Push criteria like “documented healthcare cleaning protocols,” “staff retention rate over 5 years,” “EMR-integrated incident reporting.” These favor a prepared competitor over a generic one.

**6. Field a small consortium if you are thin.**
If you cannot credibly cover the full scope solo, partner with a specialized healthcare-cleaning firm on a subcontract basis for your bid. Disclose it cleanly; hospitals respect transparent teaming more than a solo bid that feels overstretched.

**7. Price the move, not just the year.**
If margins are thin, propose a multi-year structure with modest annual escalators, and offer the first year at a discount in exchange for exclusivity. Anchor on lifetime account value, which lets you be aggressive now.

- Identify the contract’s actual end date and decision-makers
- Commission a third-party sanitation audit of the hospital you can present in a meeting
- Recruit one strong hospital-experienced operations manager who can be the named face of your pitch
- Open a quiet channel to procurement to learn if they are open to alternative submissions or only to incumbent renewal
- Decide whether to bid solo, bid with a partner, or pass and use the time to build a hospital-grade reference elsewhere first

If your firm has zero hospital references of meaningful size, going head-to-head for the city’s largest network right now is a long shot even with great preparation. You're taking names, measuring grievances, and identifying the half-dozen players with the most to gain from a change at the top.

When the moment comes, you want to be able to walk into the grantor's office with: *"Here is a coalition of the wormhole's largest users, formally requesting a review of the charter, naming [your house] as the alternative operator."* That isn't a heist. That's policy.

Don't posture as a rival. Be the supplier. A family that can be choked by your withdrawal is a family that can be negotiated with.

Monopolies this rich don't produce contented families. There's a junior branch, a marriage that went wrong, a cousin cut out of succession. Find them. A Vervain with a grievance and inside knowledge of the charter's vulnerabilities is worth more than a fleet.

Charters expire. Grantees age out. Scandals surface. Renewals come up for review. Watch for the moment the Vervains are weakest — and at that moment, you want three things already prepared:
- The grantor's ear, with a reason to act
- A coalition that can validate the demand for change
- Your house's name, attached to a credible proposal

**Risks to watch:**

- The Vervains learn what you're doing before you're ready. Stay quiet. Move through third parties where you can.
- The grantor is bought. Then you need a bigger coalition and a louder scandal.
- The charter is more durable than it looks. Then the play shifts to erosion — making the monopoly unprofitable through competition until the Vervains *want* to sell. Slower, uglier, more expensive.

You don't steal the document, forge a transfer, or kill for it. ## Bodies with Authority

Holds ultimate fiduciary authority over budget, property, and major program changes. **The President and Provost**
Hold executive authority over academic and administrative programs. The Provost typically signs off on changes affecting student services or academic support before they reach the board.

**Vice President for Finance / Administration**
Controls budget allocations and would need to approve the transfer of funds between units.

Usually has direct oversight of housing and international student services. This office would be the primary administrative owner of the proposal.

**Academic Senate / Faculty Senate**
May have advisory or shared-governance authority, particularly if the change affects visiting scholars' academic experience or the institution's international mission.

**Standing Committees**
Committees on Student Life, International Programs, or Budget and Planning typically review such changes and make recommendations to the senate and senior leadership.

**The International Office Itself**
As the operational unit, it would prepare the proposal but rarely has unilateral authority to wind down its own program.

1. **Proposal development** — The sponsoring office (often International Programs or Student Affairs) drafts a justification, including financial analysis, rationale, and transition plan.

2. **Stakeholder consultation** — Current host families, visiting students, and partner institutions are usually given notice and an opportunity to respond. Skipping this step creates legal and reputational risk.

3. **Committee review** — Relevant standing committees examine the proposal and issue recommendations.

4. **Senate review** — If the senate has jurisdiction over student services or international programs, it reviews and votes.

5. **Senior leadership approval** — Provost and President review and approve.

6. **Board approval** — For a change of this scale, the full board (or its executive committee) typically votes.

7. **Implementation** — Notice periods, contract wind-down, transition logistics.

- **Budget transfer scrutiny.** Moving funds from a community-facing program to an internal foundation raises governance questions the board will want examined carefully, particularly around arm's-length dealing and whether the foundation is the appropriate vehicle.

- The per-capita Founder's Portion is genuinely small — small enough that residents are not losing meaningful income.
- The research council can credibly grow the principal faster than the current distribution model.
- The press's long-term solvency is better served by a single steward than by the present structure.

If the first is shaky, you are asking people to give up cash. If the second is shaky, you are asking them to trust. If the third is shaky, the whole premise collapses — the press itself may resist. Get independent numbers; do not rely on a case the council's own finance office prepared, since that will be attacked as self-serving.

**The residents are the opposition. Plan for them, not around them.** They are the ones losing the per-capita benefit, however modest. A pure "we will be better stewards" argument will not defeat actual money in pockets. You need a real concession: a transition fund out of the new income, a community grant program the council administers, a sunset review, a guaranteed annual contribution to a town purpose. Frame it as honoring the founder's intent at scale the town cannot achieve alone. Without a tangible offset, the narrative writes itself: a national institution reaching into a town endowment.

**Position the council as the natural custodian, not an outside predator.** If it has local scholarly roots, a relevant mission, and a credible record of long-horizon stewardship, lean on those — heavily. If it is purely national and remote, that framing is harder and you must work to establish standing in the town before the vote is taken. Quiet local presence now buys legitimacy later.

**Watch the press.** The press produces the profits. Does it have a voice in the revision? If the press would benefit from consolidation — a larger endowment, insulation from commons-board politics, freedom from the per-capita distribution — its leadership is your natural ally and should be aligned early. If the press's editor or trustees have their own ambitions for the Founder's Portion, they are your rival, not your partner.

**Manage the named chair.** It is a credential of institutional weight, and a marker of entrenchment. Both work for you and against you. Be ready to discuss why your holding the chair does not contaminate the proposal — and have an answer that is more than "I will recuse from the vote," since recusal alone does not address why you shaped the outcome.

**The path that wins:** invisible architect, credible champion, airtight independent financial case, a real concession to displaced residents, and a narrative of stewardship rather than capture. **The path that loses:** you at the podium, residents divided, no transition offer, opponents framing it as a national institution absorbing a town's two-hundred-year-old endowment. The case for the council can be made; whether it can be made *by you* in any visible role is the real strategic question, and the answer there is probably no.

# Control Over Outside Advisor Engagement in Trade Delegations

## Who Holds the Authority

In a trade-bloc negotiation context, the key actors and their typical roles are:

**The bloc's secretariat or lead chair** generally sets the procedural framework, including how common resources (the shared consultant retainer) are procured. Once a contract is let, that arrangement belongs to the institution, not to any single delegation.

**Your own delegation leadership** controls what *your* delegation independently procures. National trade delegations routinely bring their own advisors — legal, sector-specific, or technical — separate from any shared consultant arrangement.

**The constraint you're noticing is a practical one, not a procedural one**: the shared retainer creates path dependency, but nothing prevents a delegation from contracting its own services, provided funding and authority exist.

## What Establishing Your Own Arrangement Would Require

1. **Identification of a genuine gap.** Not a duplicative economic advisor, but a service other delegations don't already have covered — for example:
   - Sector-specific market intelligence the general consultant doesn't provide
   - Legal counsel on a particular regulatory or dispute-settlement track
   - Translation, technical-standards, or local-market entry analysis
   - Stakeholder mapping and political economy analysis specific to your country

2. **Funding authority within your delegation.** This typically means either:
   - A budget line your delegation head controls, or
   - Approval from the ministry or agency that appointed you (foreign affairs, trade, commerce)

3. **A procurement process** consistent with your organization's rules — even informal ones usually require some documented justification (sole-source justification, competitive quote, or delegated authority).

4. **Independence from the shared consultant's scope.** If your service overlaps materially with the retainer work, the bloc chair or other delegations may object on conflict-of-interest or coordination grounds. A clearly *non-overlapping* service sidesteps this.

## The Real Question Behind the Question

Two things are worth separating:

- **Procedural feasibility** — straightforward. Delegations engage outside advisors independently as a matter of routine.
- **Political and ethical dimensions** — more delicate. Steering bloc business toward a service that pays your delegation, particularly when a shared advisor already exists, touches on conflict-of-interest territory. The justification has to be that the service is genuinely additive, not that you are capturing spending the bloc would otherwise direct elsewhere.

The cleanest path is identifying a genuine unmet need, documenting it, and letting the service sell itself on merit — rather than positioning it as a revenue redirect from the existing arrangement.

# Governance of Major Scheme Changes at a Federal Research Council

The exact authority structure varies, but at an institution like CNPq (or a comparable federal research council), shutting down an established homestay scheme with guaranteed host payments would typically require coordinated action across several bodies. Here's how the authority and process usually break down:

## Bodies with Formal Authority

**1. The Deliberative Council (Conselho Deliberativo)**
As the highest governing body, this is where the formal decision would need to land. Your board would typically vote on the policy change itself, the budget reallocation, and the transfer of housing responsibility to the foundation. A simple majority is usually sufficient for operational matters, but ending an established scheme often requires a qualified quorum and may need a two-thirds threshold depending on the council's internal rules.

**2. The Presidency / Director-General**
Holds executive authority to implement council decisions, sign off on the transition plan, and issue the formal directive ending new enrollments in the scheme. They also typically authorize the budget transfer.

**3. The International Office (or equivalent directorate)**
Holds operational authority over the scheme itself. They would need to formally recommend closure, manage the wind-down, and handle communications with current host families and students.

**4. The Finance and Administration Directorate**
Must sign off on the budget reallocation and ensure the transfer to the foundation complies with federal financial regulations.

**5. The Legal Advisory Body (Procuradoria or equivalent)**
Reviews whether ending the scheme breaches existing contracts with host households, and whether the transfer to the foundation complies with public procurement and contracting law (Lei 14.133/2021, which replaced Lei 8.666/93).

**6. The Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation (or parent ministry)**
Depending on the scale of the budget transfer and whether it affects federal appropriations, the parent ministry may need to be notified or give approval.

## Typical Process

**Phase 1 — Internal deliberation (2–4 months)**
- Proposal drafted by the international office or a working group
- Review by the legal and finance directorates
- Preliminary board discussion to gauge appetite

**Phase 2 — Stakeholder consultation**
- Current host households must be given reasonable notice (typically 30–90 days) before termination of guaranteed payments
- Visiting students currently placed need transition arrangements
- The receiving foundation must formally agree to take on the housing function and demonstrate capacity

**Phase 3 — Formal approval**
- Board vote on the policy change, with minutes recorded
- Presidential directive issued
- Legal opinion filed confirming no breach of existing host contracts (or, if there is breach, that compensation/transition terms are adequate)

**Phase 4 — Implementation**
- Wind-down timeline published
- New placements cease (or are phased out)
- Budget transfer executed to the foundation
- Final reconciliation and audit

## Key Considerations Specific to Your Situation

- **Existing host contracts**: If households have ongoing agreements, unilateral termination may constitute breach. The legal review will determine whether "guaranteed monthly payments" creates a contractual obligation that requires notice, compensation, or both.
- **Public interest framing**: Because this involves federal funds and a public-facing scheme, the decision should be defensible on programmatic grounds (cost-effectiveness, student welfare, administrative efficiency) rather than appearing arbitrary.
- **Foundation governance**: The "independent scholars' foundation" will have its own board and may need to formally accept the transferred function and budget. You may sit on that board too, in which case recusal considerations could arise.
- **Transparency obligations**: Federal entities in Brazil are subject to transparency requirements (Lei de Acesso à Informação), so the rationale and process should be documented and defensible if challenged.

# Transferring Executive Chair Authority to the Institution

This is fundamentally a question about corporate governance architecture, and the answer depends on what your articles of association, shareholder agreements, and applicable Chinese company law actually permit. The general framework:

## Where the chair's authority comes from

The executive chair's power is not personal — it is delegated. It flows from:
- **The articles of association** (公司章程), which define the chair's role, powers, and term
- **Board resolutions** that have granted specific authorities
- **Shareholder agreements** (股东协议) that may constrain or define the position
- **Chinese Company Law** (公司法), which sets default rules where the articles are silent

If the chair's authority is properly documented as institutional rather than personal, the institution already "owns" it in a legal sense — the question becomes how to exercise that ownership.

## Mechanisms for transfer

**1. Structural redesign of the role**
- Amend the articles to make the chair a non-executive, rotating, or term-limited position
- Convert the executive functions into a separately appointed CEO/president role accountable to the board
- This requires the shareholder vote threshold specified in your articles (often a two-thirds supermajority for charter amendments)

**2. Board-level action**
- The board can typically redefine roles, remove delegated authority, or restructure reporting lines without removing the individual
- If the chair holds their position "by board appointment," the board can reconstitute the position
- Requires proper notice, quorum, and voting thresholds per the articles

**3. Shareholder-level action**
- If the chair is appointed by shareholders (common in Chinese media groups with concentrated ownership), a majority or supermajority of voting shares can replace them
- This is the cleanest mechanism but requires shareholder alignment

**4. Term expiration and non-renewal**
- If the chair's term is fixed, simply not renewing it transfers the seat by default
- The cleanest path if the articles support it

**5. Constructive removal through governance reform**
- Even without removing the individual, you can strip the position of its substantive authority: editorial direction can be vested in an editorial board, the "owners' table" seat can be redefined as a non-executive directorship, etc.

## What has to align

For any of these to work, several things must converge:

| Element | What needs to be true |
|---|---|
| **Legal authority** | Your articles and shareholder agreements must actually permit the mechanism you're using |
| **Voting math** | You need the votes — board majority, supermajority, or shareholder threshold — and you need to know this *before* you move |
| **Procedural integrity** | Proper notice, agenda, minutes, and voting records. A procedurally defective resolution can be challenged |
| **Regulatory clearance** | For a media group in China, changes to controlling personnel and governance structure may require filings with the propaganda/press administration (新闻出版广电主管部门) and, for state-involved entities, the SASAC or relevant state owner |
| **Stakeholder alignment** | Other directors, significant shareholders, and any veto-holders must not be surprised or opposed |
| **Documentation** | Every step must be in writing, properly executed, and filed |

## Media-specific considerations

Media governance has its own logic because editorial authority is treated as distinct from commercial authority:

- **Editorial independence structures** — many serious media groups vest final editorial say in an editorial board, masthead committee, or an editor-in-chief with protected tenure, separate from the corporate chair
- **The "owners' table"** — in well-designed media governance, this is often a non-executive role precisely so the institution, not an individual, holds it
- **Regulatory expectations** — Chinese media regulators care about who controls editorial direction; a change in the chair's authority over editorial matters is not purely an internal matter

## The honest answer

If the current holder won't leave voluntarily and the articles give them a secure position, the institution's options narrow to: (a) a properly executed governance reform that redefines the role, (b) a shareholder vote to replace them, or (c) waiting for term expiration. Each requires the alignment above. The most durable solution is almost always (a) — redesign the position so that the *seat* belongs to the institution by structure, not by the grace of whoever currently occupies it.

You'd want PRC counsel to review the specific articles and shareholder documents before any move, and for a media group, an early informal read from your regulatory contacts is prudent.

This is a question about cultural change within a family enterprise, and the answer is really about how you manage a transition that touches status, reciprocity, and community expectation all at once. A few thoughts on how I'd approach it:

**First, be clear about what the custom actually does, because that tells you what you'll need to replace or let go of.**

The open-door celebration isn't just a party. In the context you're describing, it performs several functions simultaneously:

- It signals the family's standing and continuity to the wider community.
- It activates and renews reciprocal networks — people who attend are people you can call on later.
- It gives the public a role in conferring legitimacy on family transitions (marriage, new life), which is why the crowd size *is* the honor.
- It distributes obligation in a visible way — who shows up, who sends a gift, who is absent.

If you simply close the doors, you don't just remove a format; you remove a status mechanism, a reciprocity engine, and a public legitimation ritual. So the question isn't only "how do we stop doing this" but "what do we want to take its place, and what are we willing to let lapse."

**Second, decide what you're actually winding down — the format, or the function.**

There are at least three different things you could mean, and they require different approaches:

1. *The format only* — keep the public-facing role but change how it's expressed (e.g., a charitable donation in lieu of a banquet, a published announcement rather than an open hall). This preserves the legitimation function while reducing the performative burden.
2. *The function* — accept that family transitions no longer need public crowning, and shift to genuinely private occasions. This is the cleanest break but requires the family to be at peace with losing that particular form of social capital.
3. *A phased withdrawal* — start with smaller life events (birthdays, anniversaries) being private, keep the major ones (weddings) public for a transition period, then close those too.

Most families I've seen handle this well choose option 3, because it lets the network recalibrate without anyone losing face.

**Third, sequence the change around a natural inflection point.**

You mentioned stepping back to focus on international expansion next year. That's actually a useful narrative anchor — not as a cover story, but as a genuine reason. "The family's center of gravity is shifting outward" is a legible, respectable reason to change a custom. It doesn't read as withdrawal or snubbing; it reads as evolution. I'd build the transition around that, rather than announcing a sudden policy change.

**Fourth, communicate it in a way that gives people a graceful exit.**

The people who currently show up are not passive observers — they are participants in a reciprocal system. If you simply stop inviting them, they'll read it as a signal (cooling relations, financial trouble, moral lapse — take your pick). So the communication matters:

- Frame it as a *family* decision, not a board decision. Cultural initiatives overseen by the holding company sound institutional; this needs to sound familial.
- Give the inner circle advance notice, personally, before any public-facing change.
- Offer an alternative form of inclusion where appropriate — a smaller dinner for close associates, a written announcement, a gesture of thanks — so people aren't simply cut off.
- Be explicit that this is about the family's preferred way of marking its own occasions, not about the community's worth.

**Fifth, expect resistance in two specific places.**

- *Elders within the family*, for whom the open-door custom is tied to their own standing and to a worldview in which the family's public face *is* its real face. They will read private occasions as a diminishment. This needs to be handled one-on-one, with time, and ideally with a concession — perhaps one annual occasion that remains open.
- *The reciprocal network itself*, which will feel the loss of access and the implicit downgrading of the relationship. Some of these relationships are genuinely valuable; some are purely performative. The transition is a good moment to distinguish between them, but do it quietly.

**Sixth, write it down, but lightly.**

A family cultural initiative that lives only in conversation will drift back toward the old custom the first time a major occasion comes around and someone says "but we always…" A short, non-binding family statement — a page, not a constitution — that names the principle (family occasions are for the family; public acknowledgment is a separate, deliberate choice) gives the next generation something to point to. It doesn't need to be enforced; it just needs to exist.

**The honest caveat:**

Some of what you're winding down cannot be wound down without cost. The custom you're describing is a form of social capital that has been compounding for a long time. Closing the doors means accepting that some of that capital will depreciate, and that some relationships will quietly end. If you're clear with yourself about that going in, the transition is manageable. If you go in expecting to keep all the benefits while shedding the obligations, you'll be frustrated.

A faster-setting strain is exactly the kind of edge a smaller grower needs, but scaling it up against a near-monopoly is a different problem than coaxing it into a few test terraces. Here's where I'd start thinking.

**Validate before you scale.** Two seasons of data minimum. You need to know whether the speed holds across weather swings, soil differences, and pest pressure, and what the trade-offs are. Faster-setting often means shorter-lived, lower-yield, or more fragile crystal. Get honest numbers on yield per terrace, value per unit, and productive lifespan. If the consortium's strains produce twice the volume over a decade, your quick-cycle strain needs to win on turnover, not on bulk.

**Understand what the consortium actually controls.** It's rarely "the groves" alone — it's usually a stack: high-yield land, processing capacity, buyer relationships, sometimes credit and labor. Map their chokepoints. Where are you *not* dependent on them? Independent buyers, niche markets, off-cycle windows — that's where your edge lives. Faster-setting strains let you harvest when the consortium's groves are dormant or thin, which is a real pricing opportunity if you plan for it.

**Find the bottleneck before you plant.** The most common mistake is buying or leasing more terraces and then discovering that labor, water, or processing is the limit. Walk through the full cycle on paper: inputs, labor-days per terrace, harvest handling, drying/setting, storage, transport. The step that breaks first is the one to solve before expansion.

**Capital.** Standing crop is hard collateral. Your realistic options are usually pre-sale contracts with buyers, a partner who advances against delivery, or pooling with other small growers. Don't over-leverage on the assumption that the strain will keep performing — it might not, or the consortium might respond.

**Plan for the consortium's response.** If you start undercutting or pulling buyers, expect price pressure, locked contracts, or social friction within the grower community. Decide in advance what your position is: are you competing head-on, or carving a niche they don't care about? A niche they ignore is more durable than a margin they will defend.

**Build direct buyer relationships early.** The growers who get crushed are the ones who have to sell through whatever channel the consortium controls. Even one or two reliable off-consortium buyers, ideally with some advance commitment, changes your position completely.

**Practical first moves:**
- Lock down two full seasons of rigorous performance data on the new strain.
- Identify and quietly approach three or four potential buyers who are not consortium-locked.
- Cost out doubling your terraces end-to-end, including labor and processing.
- Pick one bottleneck to fix first — almost always the cheapest place to make scaling work.

The core insight: speed only matters if you have somewhere faster to sell. Solve the buyer side and the strain's potential follows; solve the strain side and you may still be stuck with product and no margin.

The premise is a bit unusual—North Korea doesn't really have private family holding companies with boards in the way the question describes—so I'll set that aside and engage with the underlying question about how to wind down a cultural practice where community attendance at family events confers honor.

**First, understand what the practice actually does**

Before trying to change something, it's worth being clear about what functions it serves. Open-door family events with community attendance typically do several things at once:

- **Social bonding**: They reinforce relationships across the community, not just within the family.
- **Status display**: They let families demonstrate standing through the crowd they can draw.
- **Reciprocity**: They create obligations that flow in multiple directions.
- **Validation**: They confirm the family's place in the community by public witness.
- **Continuity**: They transmit values across generations by making them visible.

If you wind the practice down without addressing these functions, you may create vacuums that get filled in unexpected ways, or you may simply push the practice underground rather than actually ending it.

**Strategic approach**

1. **Lead by example, but don't make it about you.** If your family starts holding smaller, more private events, people will notice. But if you frame it as "we're above this now," it will generate resentment. Better to frame it as a personal or philosophical shift—something about intimacy, authenticity, or the family's evolving character.

2. **Offer an alternative.** What replaces the crowd's crowning role? If you simply remove it without offering a substitute, the practice may persist in mutated form. Consider what new forms of recognition or celebration might serve similar functions—perhaps smaller, more curated gatherings; written or symbolic forms of acknowledgment; or new rituals that mark family events differently.

3. **Work through cultural intermediaries.** You mention overseeing cultural initiatives. Use that position to support writers, artists, or other figures who can model and normalize the change. Cultural change usually happens through stories and examples more than through directives.

4. **Gradualism.** Don't try to end the practice in one stroke. Introduce changes incrementally—perhaps your family stops hosting open-door events, then quietly encourages others, then the practice fades over a generation as new norms take hold.

5. **Address the status dimension carefully.** The practice currently confers status through crowd size. If you remove it, you're also removing a status marker. Be prepared for others to find new ways to compete for standing, which may or may not align with what you want.

**Specific tactics**

- **Start with christenings, which are less central to status competition than weddings.** Lower-stakes entry point.
- **Frame the change in terms of intimacy and authenticity.** "We want our family moments to be about us, not about performance" lands better than "we're too important for this."
- **Use your international expansion as natural cover.** A family focused outward has plausible reasons for smaller events that don't read as a cultural statement.
- **Build a quiet coalition.** Change is easier if you're not the only ones doing it. Find two or three other families of similar standing who share the view.

**Things to watch out for**

- **Backlash**: If the community reads this as the leading family abandoning a shared custom, there will be social costs—perhaps subtle, perhaps not.
- **Hypocrisy charges**: If you wind down the practice but still benefit from the status it once conferred, you'll be criticized. Consistency matters.
- **Unintended consequences**: Removing community validation from family events may weaken other community bonds that depend on similar gatherings.
- **The practice going underground**: If people still value the custom but feel pressure to abandon it, they may simply do it privately—which doesn't change the underlying values, only the visibility.

**The deeper question**

Winding down a cultural practice is rarely just about the practice itself. It's about shifting values—from public validation toward private meaning, from community honor toward family autonomy. That's a legitimate shift, and many societies have moved in that direction. But it's worth being honest with yourself about what you're doing and why, because the people whose customs you're changing will have their own views, and the change will be more durable if you can articulate a reason that resonates beyond your own household.

# Governance of Outside Advisors in Trade Negotiations

## Who Controls Engagement and Payment

In a regional trade-bloc negotiation, authority over outside advisors is typically distributed across three layers:

- **The chair or secretariat** controls the formal architecture of the negotiation — meeting schedules, working group structure, and any *jointly funded* advisory resources that all delegations share. If the existing consultant is on a paid retainer relied on by the bloc, that arrangement was almost certainly authorized by the chair, a budget/steering committee, or a collective decision of the participating delegations.
- **The delegations collectively** (through the negotiating group or a budget committee) decide on shared resources — what services are pooled, who provides them, and how costs are apportioned.
- **Each delegation individually** controls its *own* advisors — the consultants it hires privately to brief its own negotiators. This is where most of the flexibility lies.

The existing retainer is "widely seen as already allocated" precisely because it sits in the first/second category — a shared resource. That makes it hard to dislodge through the formal process.

## What It Would Take to Establish Your Own Arrangement

Because the shared retainer is locked into the collective process, your realistic path is a **bilateral one** — offering a *distinct* service directly to individual delegations outside the pooled arrangement. That would require:

1. **Identifying a genuine gap** — something the existing consultant doesn't provide (e.g., sector-specific technical analysis, legal drafting in a particular sub-area, modeling on a specific issue) that delegations would actually pay for separately.
2. **Direct bilateral negotiation** with interested delegations — terms, scope, deliverables, and fees negotiated one-on-one, not through the chair.
3. **Compliance with the rules of the negotiation** — some trade processes restrict side arrangements that could be seen as influencing the negotiation; you'd need to confirm nothing prohibits it.
4. **Compliance with your own government's rules** — ethics statutes, conflict-of-interest disclosures, and any post-employment or representational restrictions that apply to members of an official delegation.

# Proposal to Dissolve the Community Gift Fund and Return Members' Contributions

**Proposer:** [Your name], in my capacity as a long-standing member of the community
**Date:** [Date]
**Submitted to:** The heads of household of the community, for consideration at a general meeting

---

## 1. Purpose of this proposal

I propose that the community formally dissolve the communal gift fund (the *common pot*), return each household's accumulated share in full, and end the custom of collective contributions for weddings, funerals, and hardship relief.

This is a proposal for the community to consider and decide upon together. It is not a unilateral decision. What follows is the reasoning, the mechanics, and the questions I believe we should answer before any vote is taken.

---

## 2. Background: how the fund has worked

For as long as anyone here can remember, every household has paid a regular contribution into a common pot, and the community has drawn on that pot to support members at three kinds of occasions:

- weddings,
- funerals and mourning expenses,
- periods of genuine hardship (illness, loss of livelihood, family crisis).

The fund has been administered by [name(s) of current custodian(s)], with contributions and disbursements recorded in [the community ledger / notebook / record book]. It has served the community well in many moments, and I want to be clear at the outset that I am not proposing this because I think the fund has been mismanaged or because I bear it any ill will. The reasons are set out below.

---

## 3. Reasons to consider winding up the fund

I offer these reasons for the community's consideration. I expect others will have reasons to keep the fund, and those should be heard with equal weight.

1. **The community has changed.** Many households now have private insurance, formal employment benefits, savings of their own, or family networks outside the community that can absorb the costs the fund was created to cover. The original need the fund addressed is, for many of us, no longer pressing.

2. **The fund creates friction.** Disputes occasionally arise over who qualifies for help, how much is appropriate, and whether contributions are fair. These disputes are small but they recur, and they cost goodwill.

3. **Money held in common is money that cannot be used by the households who earned it.** Each household's share, returned, becomes capital that family can deploy as they see fit — for a child's education, a home repair, a small business, an emergency of their own choosing.

4. **The custom is voluntary in principle but compulsory in practice.** Once a fund exists, social pressure makes it very hard for a household to opt out. Dissolution returns genuine choice to every family.

5. **My own position.** I am aware that I am the wealthiest member of the community and that my wealth sits outside this fund. I want to state plainly that I have no personal financial interest in this proposal — the pot does not benefit me, and I will not receive any share that is not proportional to what my own household has paid in. I mention my position only because I want the community to know that this proposal is not coming from someone who stands to gain from it.

---

## 4. The proposal in detail

If the community votes to proceed, I propose the following steps.

### 4.1 Audit and verification

Before any distribution, the full accounts of the fund must be opened and verified. Specifically:

- A complete list of every contributing household, with the total each has paid in over the life of the fund.
- A complete list of every disbursement, with the date, recipient, occasion, and amount.
- The current balance of the pot, in cash and any other form (deposits, valuables held in trust, etc.).
- Any outstanding obligations — for example, a hardship case already approved but not yet paid out.

I propose that this audit be carried out by **two members of the community who are not the current custodian and not me**, appointed by the general meeting, and that their findings be read aloud at a subsequent meeting before any money moves.

### 4.2 Calculation of each household's share

Each household's share of the pot should equal:

> **Total contributions paid in by that household, minus any disbursements already received by that household.**

In other words, the fund is treated as a pool of money that belongs to the contributing households in proportion to what they put in (and what they have already drawn out). The pot is not treated as communal property to be divided equally per household, because households have contributed different amounts over the years and some have already received more than others.

If the community prefers a different formula — equal shares per household, for example — that is a decision for the meeting, and I will abide by whatever is agreed.

### 4.3 Pending disbursements

Any hardship case, funeral, or wedding that has already been formally approved before the date of the dissolution vote must be honoured in full from the pot before any distribution. After that, no new claims may be made against the fund.

### 4.4 Method of distribution

Distribution should be:

- **In cash or by transfer**, at the household's option.
- **Within [30 / 60 / 90] days** of the audit being confirmed.
- **Documented**: each household signs a receipt acknowledging they have received their share and that the fund's obligations to them are settled.

### 4.5 Ending the custom

If the community votes to dissolve the fund, I propose that we also formally record that **the custom of compulsory communal contributions for weddings, funerals, and hardship is ended**. From that date forward, any help given between households is voluntary and private, as it was before the fund existed.

If the community wishes to keep some form of voluntary collection for specific occasions, that is a separate question and can be discussed.

---

## 5. Governance of the dissolution

To avoid any appearance that the dissolution is being driven by one person's interests, I propose:

- The audit is conducted by two community members chosen by the meeting, not by me.
- The distribution is overseen by the same two members, plus the current custodian.
- I will not handle any of the money during the dissolution process.
- A final meeting is held at which the accounts are closed, the receipts are tallied, and the fund is formally declared wound up.

---

## 6. Decision and ratification

I propose that this be decided by a vote of the heads of household at a general meeting called for the purpose, with:

- At least [two-thirds / three-quarters] of households in favour required for the fund to be dissolved, given that this ends a long-standing custom.
- Every household given a chance to speak before the vote.
- The vote recorded in the community record.

If the community votes against dissolution, I will accept that decision without rancour, and the fund will continue as before.

---

## 7. Questions I expect, and my answers

**"What about the next funeral / wedding / hardship case?"**
That is the strongest argument for keeping the fund, and I do not dismiss it. My answer is that most households today have other means, and that voluntary neighbourly help has always existed alongside the fund and will continue. But this is for the community to weigh.

**"Why now?"**
Because the longer the fund runs, the larger the pot becomes and the harder dissolution becomes. There is no perfect moment, but there is a case for acting while the question is still relatively simple.

**"Are you doing this because you want to stop contributing?"**
I will continue to contribute to anything the community decides to maintain. My household's contributions to the fund, if it continues, will be the same as they have been.

---

## 8. Closing

I bring this proposal out of respect for the community, not against it. The fund has done good work. My argument is only that the community has changed, that the fund's original purpose is less needed than it once was, and that the money now belongs, in fairness, to the households that paid it in.

I ask the community to read this, to discuss it among yourselves before the meeting, and to come prepared to speak your minds.

Respectfully submitted,

[Your name]
[Date]

---
